The collapse of the nine-storey Rana Plaza building at Savar, near Dhaka in Bangladesh, on 24 April 2013. It killed 1,134 people, most of them women garment workers, and injured about 2,500. It is the deadliest disaster in the history of the garment industry.

The building housed several garment factories making clothes for well-known Western brands, as well as shops and a bank. It had upper floors built without permits on soft ground. Cracks appeared the day before; the shops and bank closed, but factory managers ordered workers back in. The next morning, after a power cut, heavy generators started up and the building gave way.

Garment exports are the core of Bangladesh's economy and employ millions, mostly women. The disaster drew attention to the safety of cheap "fast fashion". Within weeks, brands and unions signed the Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh, later joined by some two hundred companies, which brought independent inspections of thousands of factories. The building's owner was jailed. Like the Bhopal disaster in India, it became a symbol of the human cost of industry in poor countries.
